Rewrite the following essay substantively. Aim for 1305 words; the acceptable range is 1044-1500 words, and the corpus-wide hard range is 800-1500 words. Use at least 6 natural paragraphs, preferably approximately 6 paragraphs. Do not include a heading.

SOURCE ESSAY:
T HE recently established chair in the history, literature, and institutions of the United States which is to be shared among the several universities of Great Britain, is quite different from the exchange professorships of sometimes unhappy memory. It is not at all the idea to carry over one of our professors each year and indoctrinate him with the true culture at its source. The occupant of the chair will be, if the announced intention is carried out, quite as often British as American, and quite as likely a public man as a professor. The chief object is to bring to England a better knowledge of the United States, and a purpose more laudable can scarcely be imagined. Peace and prosperity will endure in the world in some very precise relation to the extent to which England succeeds in understanding us.

It is not an illusion to suppose that our understanding of the British is on the whole better than theirs of us. The British Empire is a large and comparatively simple fact, now conspicuously before the world for a long time. The United States was, in British eyes, until recently, a comparatively insignificant fact, yet vastly more complicated than they imagined. Each, of course, perfectly knew the faults of the other, assessed with an unerring cousinly eye. The American bragged in a nasal whine, the Briton patronized in a throaty burble. Whoever among the struggling nations of the world might win, England saw to it that she never lost; your Yankee was content with the more ignoble triumphs of merchandising, willing to cheapen life if he could only add to his dollars. But the excellence of English political institutions and methods, the charm of English life, the tremendous power of the Empire for promoting freedom and civilization in the world, these are things which Americans have long recognized and in a way understood. Anything like an equivalent British appreciation of America in the large seems confined to a very few honorable exceptions among them. Admiration for Niagara, which is half British anyway, or enthusiasm for the "Wild West"— your better-class Englishman always thrills to the frontier—is no step at all toward rightly appreciating America.

To no inconsiderable extent this is America's own fault. She does not present to the world a record that is easily read. It is obvious, for instance—and so obvious that it is not often enough stated—that America has and will continue to have a fundamentally English civilization. English law is the basis of her law. English speech is her speech, and if with a difference, it is a difference that the philologist, all things considered, finds amazingly small. English literature is her literature—Chaucer and Shakespeare hers because her blood then coursed indistinguishably through the English heart they knew so well; Milton, Dryden, and the Queen Anne men hers, because she was still a part of England; the later men hers by virtue of affectionate acquaintanceship and a generous and not inconsiderable rivalry. English history, in short, is her history. The struggles of the thirteenth century through which law and parliament came into being, the struggles of the seventeenth century through which law and parliament came to rule, are America's struggles upon which she can look back with the satisfaction that some things that have been done in the world need never be undone or done over again, whatever the room for improvement may still be. Americans, no less than British, recognize that independence was largely an accidental result of a war which sprang out of a false theory of economics, but whose conclusion carried with it a lesson in the management of empire which subsequent history shows the British to have learned thoroughly and for the benefit of all concerned. American independence, however, once established, pointed a way to democratic freedom which England hastened to follow. This we know. And yet—

And yet we allow these obvious and fundamental considerations to become marvelously obscured. We allow England's failure to solve an insoluble Irish problem to arouse in us an attitude of mind possibly excusable in some Irishmen, but wholly inexcusable in any American. We allow a sentimental regard for some immigrant from Eastern Europe, who comes to us with a philosophy born of conditions that in English-speaking lands ceased to be centuries ago, to make us pretend to see in him the true expression of America's traditional ideals. We allow ourselves to be far too easy with the phrase, "He is not pro-German, he is merely anti-British." Why are they anti-British? Why should they be permitted to make it falsely appear that recognition of the English basis of America involves approval of everything that England in her history may or may not have done? Why should they be allowed to pretend that disapproval of some particular act of England justifies repudiation of most of the things by virtue of which we are what we are? America from the first has been part of the great English experiment—great because it is capable of learning from experience.

The world has put a big investment in blood and treasure, and all that they imply, into the education of England. It is satisfied—the world's response to Germany's insolent challenge is the proof of it—that its pains have been well bestowed. England is more nearly fit than any other nation to wield the power that is hers. That is not to deny the peculiar virtues of other nations; indeed, these virtues have largely contributed to the result. Italy has educated her; France has educated her; we have done something; and Germany. In result, she is not perfect—the English would perhaps least of all assert that—but she has learned a great deal and held herself steady while she learned it. It is a bigger job than the world cares to undertake to teach any other nation so much. Nor would it be at all likely to succeed so well. For what England has to offer the world in return is not simply her institutions; it is not merely a formula for the effective discharge of police duty throughout the world; it is the English freeman, whether he hail from Canada, Australia, Africa, or the uttermost isles of the sea.

A most adaptable fellow, this freeman, doing all sorts of work everywhere, and with tremendous powers of assimilation. Consider him in his origins. He began by assimilating fully his own weight in Danes, while remaining an English freeman. He then perforce accepted a Norman king, as he had accepted a Danish one, hoping, as always, that the king would not trouble him too much. But when Norman William, who was very ill-informed about the breed, killed off most of his natural leaders and harried the rest into villeiny, how did he manage in a small matter of two hundred years or so to make an English gentleman not only of himself but of all the rag-tag of adventurers who had come over with William and since? How did he contrive, out of a band of exiles fleeing from an Egypt of ecclesiastical tyranny, broken younger sons, artisans out of a job, speculators, bondmen, Swedes, Dutchmen, and what not, to make America? Is he one likely to lose his bearings when in his America the age-old problem again heaves in view? This is a job he has been working at pretty successfully for more than a thousand years. Grant him a moment to realize himself afresh in the face of it. Don't expect him to stop and give a coherent explanation of what he is doing. He wouldn't be the true son of the English tradition that he is if he could do that. Perhaps the occupants of the new chair can do something of the sort for him.

message.content:
The newly created chair focusing on the history, literature, and institutions of the United States, which will be shared among various universities in Great Britain, marks a significant departure from the previous exchange professorships that often yielded mixed results. The intent is not to send an American professor annually to Britain to instill them with the “true” culture from its source. Instead, the individual holding this chair will likely be British as often as they are American, and may very well be a public figure rather than an academic. The primary goal is to foster a deeper understanding of the United States in England, and such an aspiration is indeed noble. The ongoing peace and prosperity in the world hinges significantly on how well England comprehends America.

It is a misconception to believe that American understanding of British culture is on par with British understanding of American life. The British Empire represents a substantial and relatively straightforward reality, one that has been in the global spotlight for an extended period. Conversely, the United States, until quite recently, was viewed by the British as a minor entity, albeit a far more intricate one than they assumed. Both sides are acutely aware of each other’s shortcomings, judged through a distinctly familial lens. Americans tend to boast in a nasal tone, while Britons often adopt a condescending manner. Regardless of which nation might emerge victorious in the tumultuous world stage, England ensured its own survival; the American, on the other hand, often settled for the less dignified victories found in commerce, willing to compromise quality of life for financial gain. Nonetheless, Americans have long acknowledged and appreciated the strengths of English political systems, the allure of English living, and the Empire's significant role in fostering freedom and civilization globally. This acknowledgment, however, appears to be reciprocated only by a select few notable British individuals who demonstrate a genuine admiration for America.

To a considerable degree, this lack of mutual appreciation can be attributed to America’s own shortcomings. The nation does not present a narrative that is easily deciphered. It is evident—and so plainly that it is often overlooked—that America is bound to an English heritage. English law forms the foundation of American jurisprudence. The English language, while distinct, is fundamentally similar, as even philologists acknowledge the relatively minor differences. The literary canon of America is deeply rooted in English tradition—Chaucer and Shakespeare are as much part of America’s literary fabric as they are of England's, for the shared ancestry flows through the veins of both. The turmoil of the thirteenth century that birthed law and parliament in England is mirrored in America’s own historical struggles, providing a sense of pride in the realization that certain foundational achievements need not be repeated, even as we recognize the potential for ongoing improvement. Americans, like the British, acknowledge that their independence stemmed largely from a war fueled by misguided economic theories, yet the resolution of this conflict imparted invaluable lessons in empire management—lessons that the British have adeptly learned for the collective benefit of all. The establishment of American independence, once achieved, paved the way for a democratic freedom that England was quick to embrace. We are aware of these connections, yet—

Yet, somehow, we allow these fundamental truths to become obscured. We permit the failure of England to resolve the seemingly insurmountable Irish question to foster attitudes among some Americans that are understandable for certain Irish individuals but wholly unjustifiable for any American. We allow ourselves to be swayed by an emotional attachment to an immigrant from Eastern Europe, who arrives with a worldview shaped by circumstances long since passed in English-speaking nations, leading us to mistakenly perceive them as the embodiment of America’s foundational ideals. We too readily accept the rationale of “He is not pro-German; he simply opposes British policies.” However, we must question: why is there such anti-British sentiment? Why should we allow it to appear as though recognizing the English roots of America equates to endorsing every action taken by England throughout its history? Why should dissent against specific British actions lead to a wholesale rejection of the core principles that define who we are? From the very beginning, America has been an integral part of the grand English experiment—one that is significant for its capacity to learn through experience.

The international community has invested heavily, in terms of both blood and resources, in the education of England. The world’s collective response to Germany’s audacious challenge demonstrates that this investment has been well-placed. England stands as the nation best equipped to exercise the power it possesses. This assertion does not dismiss the unique strengths of other nations; indeed, these distinct qualities have played a vital role in shaping England’s journey. Italy, France, the United States, and even Germany have all contributed to this educational endeavor. While England may not be flawless—her own citizens would likely be the first to acknowledge this—she has gleaned much from her experiences and maintained her steadiness throughout the process. Educating another nation to such a degree is a daunting task, one that the world may hesitate to undertake again. The likelihood of achieving similar results elsewhere is slim, as what England offers the globe extends beyond her institutions; it encompasses the English freeman, who can come from Canada, Australia, Africa, or the farthest reaches of the ocean.

This freeman is remarkably adaptable, excelling in various roles across the globe and exhibiting an extraordinary ability to assimilate. Reflect on his origins: he began by fully integrating the Danes into his identity while retaining the essence of an English man. He subsequently accepted a Norman king, just as he had with his Danish predecessor, with the hope that this ruler would not impose too many burdens upon him. However, when the uninformed Norman William exterminated many of his natural leaders and subjugated the remainder, how did this Englishman manage, within a span of two centuries, to elevate himself and his fellow adventurers into the status of English gentlemen? How did he transform a motley group of exiles fleeing ecclesiastical oppression, broken younger sons, unemployed artisans, speculators, and assorted immigrants into the foundation of America? Is this individual likely to lose his sense of purpose when faced with the age-old dilemmas that resurface? This is a challenge he has been navigating successfully for over a millennium. Allow him the opportunity to rediscover his identity in the context of these challenges. Do not expect him to pause and articulate a coherent rationale for his actions; he would not be a true adherent of the English tradition if he could do so. Perhaps those who take on the responsibilities of the new chair can assist him in articulating this journey.
